text: Antonio Scotti (25 January 1866 – 26 February 1936) was an Italian baritone who served as a principal artist at the New York Metropolitan Opera for more than 33 seasons and achieved great success at London's Royal Opera House, Covent Garden, and Milan's La Scala. Born in Naples, Italy, Scotti was initially intended for the priesthood but chose instead to pursue a career in opera, receiving early vocal training from Esther Trifari-Paganini and Vincenzo Lombardi. He made his debut at Malta's Theatre Royal in 1889 as Amonasro in Giuseppe Verdi's Aida and subsequently performed at various Italian opera houses, gaining stage experience in Spain, Portugal, Russia, and South America, including Buenos Aires (1891–1894 and 1897), Río de Janeiro (1893), Chile (1898), and Montevideo. In 1898, he debuted at La Scala, Milan, as Hans Sachs in Richard Wagner's Die Meistersinger, a role that later seemed unusual given his career focus. His American debut occurred in the autumn of 1899 in Chicago, followed by his first appearance in New York City on 27 December 1899 at the Metropolitan Opera in the title role of Mozart's Don Giovanni. He became a favorite at the Met, praised for his graceful singing of Donizetti's bel canto and elegant interpretations of Verdi and verismo roles. He also performed at Covent Garden in London in 1899 and returned there multiple times before World War I. In 1901, Scotti became the first baritone to sing Scarpia in the American premiere of Giacomo Puccini's Tosca at the Met and appeared in the American premieres of several operas, including Adriana Lecouvreur, Le donne curiose, Fedora, L'Oracolo, and Messaline. He performed a wide range of baritone roles such as Rigoletto, Malatesta, Belcore, Iago, Falstaff, Marcello, and Sharpless, often performing opposite his close friend Enrico Caruso, including in the title role of Rigoletto when Caruso made his Met debut as the Duke of Mantua in November 1903. Scotti partnered 15 different Toscas during his Met career. In 1912, his arrival in the U.S. with Pasquale Amato and William Hinshaw drew extensive newspaper coverage, and during that year he met restaurateur Salvatore Scoleri, who opened an Italian restaurant named after Scotti in Cincinnati, Ohio. He performed regularly at Covent Garden until 1910, with additional appearances in the 1913–1914 season, becoming London's first Scarpia and first Sharpless in Puccini's Madama Butterfly (in 1900 and 1905, respectively), roles he also performed at the Met's premiere in 1907. In 1917, he was elected an honorary member of Phi Mu Alpha Sinfonia at the New England Conservatory of Music. Scotti performed in Paris at the Opéra Comique in 1904 and 1910, singing Tosca with Emma Eames and Emilio De Marchi (conducted by Cleofonte Campanini) and with Geraldine Farrar and Leon Beyle (conducted by Gino Marinuzzi). In 1910, at the Theatre du Châtelet with the Metropolitan ensemble, he sang Falstaff conducted by Arturo Toscanini and performed the third act of La bohème in a gala with Caruso and Farrar. In 1898, he sang Don Giovanni at Salzburg with Lilli Lehmann (Donna Ana), Johanna Gadski (Donna Elvira), and Geraldine Farrar (Zerlina), conducted by Karl Muck. In 1919, Scotti formed his own troupe, the Scotti Opera Company, which he managed for several seasons while touring the United States. On 24 January 1924, he celebrated his 25th anniversary at the Met with a gala performance of Tosca. By 1930, his voice had declined significantly, but he continued to appear on the Met's roster due to his strong histrionic ability. His final performance at the Metropolitan Opera was on 20 January 1933, when he sang Chim-Fen in Franco Leoni's L'Oracolo—a role he had created in London in 1905. After resigning from the Met, Scotti returned to Italy and died in Naples three years later, in 1936, at the age of 70. A live recording from 1903 on faint and mold-damaged Mapleson Cylinders captures Scotti singing excerpts from Scarpia's music in Tosca, with soprano Emma Eames and tenor Emilio De Marchi, conducted by Luigi Mancinelli. On another undamaged Mapleson recording, he is clearly heard leading the entrance of the players in the second act of Pagliacci. From 1902 until the outbreak of hostilities in Europe in 1914, Scotti made commercial recordings for the British Gramophone and Typewriter Company, the American Victor Talking Machine Company, and the Columbia Phonograph Company. These recordings, mostly reissued on LP and CD, include solo arias and operatic duets and ensembles with Caruso, Marcella Sembrich, and Geraldine Farrar. His records demonstrate that he was a stylish, well-trained, and aristocratic singer with a smooth, steady tone and accurate execution of difficult vocal ornaments, though his voice was not especially large or resonant. A strikingly handsome and extroverted performer both on and off stage, Scotti was skilled in portraying both dramatic and comic characters.
